title: Nuclear Weapons Waste Made Workers Sick. Despite a Law Meant to Help, the DOE Keeps Fighting Their Claims.
author: Brandon Block
content:
Lonnie Rouse shuffled into a wood-paneled conference room at the Washington
state Capitol in March 2018. It had been nearly a decade since medical experts
diagnosed him with a neurological disease they attributed to his exposure to
chemicals at work. In the time since, he had acquired a stutter, begun limping
and lost several teeth biting into a banana.

For nearly 20 years, Rouse had packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive
waste at the [Hanford Site](https://www.hanford.gov/), a now-decommissioned
Department of Energy nuclear weapons production plant in south-central
Washington and one of the most contaminated nuclear sites in the country.
Tanks full of radioactive sludge exposed him to at least [48 potentially
hazardous
chemicals](https://www.hanford.gov/tocpmm/files.cfm/IHTechBasis_RPP-22491Rev1.pdf).
The worksite was so toxic, he said, that the floor once melted the rubber off
his boots.

Rouse was among the thousands of workers responsible for the ongoing
environmental cleanup at Hanford, which has been underway since the DOE shut
down the last reactor in the late 1980s. Congress [has
acknowledged](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/owcp/energy/regs/compliance/law/EEOICPAALL.pdf),
based on voluminous studies, that radiation at DOE sites poses health risks to
workers.

Over time, some people at Hanford became so sick they could no longer work.
Like Rouse, they filed for workers’ compensation. The DOE consistently
challenged their claims and tried to shift the blame onto the workers
themselves.

By the time Rouse took his place behind then-Gov. Jay Inslee, he was
desperate. His 2009 workers’ compensation claim had been denied. He had burned
through his retirement savings and declared bankruptcy.

As he watched, the governor signed [a
bill](https://lawfilesext.leg.wa.gov/biennium/2017-18/Pdf/Bills/Session%20Laws/House/1723-S.SL.pdf?q=20261021094915)
that was supposed to change his life.

![A scuffed-up photo of a man in a hazmat suit
cleaning.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261013-Albaugh-Hanford-Nuclear-Workers-
Comp-261013-0009_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)Rouse
hung onto an old photo of himself cleaning rodent feces while working at the
Hanford Site. Rouse packaged plutonium and monitored radioactive waste at the
site for almost 20 years. Image photographed by Margaret Albaugh for
ProPublica

For years, Hanford employees filing workers’ compensation claims had to prove
the chemicals they were exposed to on the job made them sick. The new law
Inslee signed flipped that burden of proof. Under [the
law](https://app.leg.wa.gov/billsummary/?BillNumber=1723&Year=2017&Initiative=false),
agencies were instructed to presume that working at Hanford had caused
[certain cancers, neurological diseases and respiratory
illnesses](https://lawfilesext.leg.wa.gov/biennium/2017-18/Pdf/Bills/Session%20Laws/House/1723-S.SL.pdf?q=20261019230918).
Now the Department of Energy would have to prove to the state that something
_other_ than the job had made the workers sick if it wanted to deny their
claims.

Rouse thought the presumption law would speed up his claim for benefits. State
lawmakers and the former governor thought it would force the DOE to take
responsibility for the harm Hanford workers were experiencing.

But despite the law, the DOE continues to fight new and existing claims,
Cascade PBS and ProPublica found. We asked the state for claims records going
back to the presumption law’s passage in 2018, but the state only provided
records going back three and a half years, to 2023. In that period, workers
filed 102 new claims for benefits, state data shows. The DOE did not recommend
approving a single one.

The state, which has final say, overruled the DOE and approved 75% of those
claims. The DOE appealed all but seven of those approvals.

Cascade PBS and ProPublica spoke to workers, surviving family members, lawyers
representing workers and state officials. They all pointed to a pattern: The
DOE systematically challenges and then drags out workers’ compensation claims
for years with recommended denials and subsequent legal appeals. Along the
way, it has spent millions on outside lawyers and expert testimony, including
doctor evaluations that point to other causes for workers’ illnesses.

The DOE has paid out benefits to Hanford workers in some cases, lawyers and
families said, but it has done so while still actively appealing the claims.
It warns workers that they may have to pay the money back.  

Our reporting found that not even death ends the cycle of appeals. About 152
workers’ claims remain stranded in this legal limbo — approved by the state
but still under appeal by the DOE. Half of those workers are dead. The DOE
continues to fight to deny their families survivors’ benefits.

“It seems pretty coldhearted, calculated, that they’re trying to save money on
the back of sick workers who they made sick,” said Gerry Pollet, one of the
Washington state representatives who sponsored the 2018 presumption law, who
is also a co-founder of the Hanford cleanup watchdog group Heart of America
Northwest. “That’s why we needed a state law.”

After Cascade PBS and ProPublica raised questions about the DOE’s pattern of
litigating claims, regulators at the Washington State Department of Labor and
Industries met twice with DOE staff, state agency spokesperson Carrie
McCausland said. But she could not point to any other actions the agency has
taken beyond the two meetings.

“Agency staff are concerned and are right now assessing the severity of
patterns we’ve seen,” McCausland wrote in an email.

The DOE did not answer detailed questions or respond to the newsrooms’
findings. In a statement, a spokesperson wrote that the DOE is following “all
applicable local, state, and federal laws” and “has a long and successful
record of accomplishment of protecting human health and the environment.”

The DOE has the right to file multiple appeals against a claim. According to
court records, its appeals have sought to overturn claims approved by the
state, narrow the period of back wages, or block survivors’ benefits, among
other things. In appeals filings, the DOE’s lawyers have argued that factors
other than work at Hanford played a role in the workers’ illnesses, including
smoking, drinking, obesity or genetics.

In Rouse’s case, the energy department blamed alcoholism and family conflicts.
The state agency that handles appeals did not find those arguments persuasive.
DOE awarded Rouse most of his back pay in 2024, his lawyer said. Rouse
declined to say how much that was, but said he is not touching the money until
the legal process concludes.

![A woman holds a blood pressure cuff while Lonnie Rouse raises his arm to
allow her to put the cuff on.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261013-Albaugh-Hanford-Nuclear-Workers-
Comp-261013-0033_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)Rouse’s
wife, Melinda, takes his vital signs. Margaret Albaugh for ProPublica

In the nearly eight years it has been fighting his claim, the DOE has filed
more than 20 appeals contesting different aspects of his claim.

“We were always told that nothing is out here that's going to harm you — you
do what you are supposed to do, and you do what you are trained to do, and
you're going to be fine,” said Rouse, who now receives 24-hour care.

“But that's not what happens.”

### “Depleted and Disgusted”  

The smell of ammonia serves as a warning, workers say, that the underground
tanks holding a mix of radioactive sludge have burped chemical vapors into the
air above. From 1998 to 2008, it was Rouse’s job to monitor the toxic waste
held in the “tank farms.” The containers together hold more than 50 million
gallons of liquid waste. Rouse says he lost count of how many times tanks
released toxic vapor that took his breath away, sometimes knocking him to the
ground and making him vomit and bleed from his nose. According to [a 2014
report
funded](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/568adf4125981deb769d96b2/t/57913722f5e2317b4dd7fb7f/1469134632092/Hanford_TVAT_Report_2014-10-30-FINAL.pdf)
by the federal government, tank farm workers exposed to chemical vapors
commonly reported nausea, headaches and nosebleeds.

The liquid sloshing around in those tanks represented the radioactive
byproducts of the Cold War. Hanford produced two-thirds of the plutonium for
the nation's nuclear arsenal and fueled the atomic bomb dropped on Nagasaki,
Japan, in 1945.

![A black-and-white aerial photo of a plant with a tall smokestack and many
big and small buildings. It sits in a dry environment next to a wide
river.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Hanford_DOE_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=2560)The
Columbia River flows by nuclear reactors at the Hanford Site in Washington
state in 1960. Department of Energy

The end of production in the late 1980s launched a cleanup effort that is
expected to continue until at least 2086. As of January 2025, more than 13,000
people were working at Hanford, nearly all of them for private companies
contracted by the DOE. It is one of the largest and most expensive efforts to
remediate toxic waste in the nation’s history.

In 2000, Congress passed the [Energy Employees Occupational Illness
Compensation Program
Act](https://www.dol.gov/sites/dolgov/files/owcp/energy/regs/compliance/law/EEOICPAALL.pdf),
which provides medical care and one-time payouts to workers at DOE sites
across the country. It was an acknowledgement that the nation’s nuclear
weapons workers had been exposed to radioactive substances known to cause
cancer. In it, lawmakers referred to a DOE policy “to litigate occupational
illness claims, which has deterred workers from filing workers’ compensation
claims and has imposed major financial burdens for such employees who have
sought compensation.”

But the benefits of the federal program were limited: It capped payouts at
$400,000.

Washington's workers’ compensation system, by contrast, can provide steady
wage replacement or a pension benefit, in some cases, for the rest of an
injured employee’s life. It’s a program that can easily surpass the maximum
federal benefit.

The state went further with its 2018 presumption law. Such laws generally
protect firefighters who are regularly exposed to smoke, burned plastics and
extreme heat. The National Council on Compensation Insurance, the Washington
state attorney general and Pollet all said they were unaware of any other
state that has extended that protection for radiological workers.

The federal government challenged Washington’s state law later that year in
court, arguing it was discriminatory because it only applied to Hanford and
the DOE.

Anticipating a Supreme Court decision that ultimately agreed, lawmakers passed
[an expanded
version](https://app.leg.wa.gov/billsummary?BillNumber=5890&Initiative=false&Year=2021)
that covered all workers at “radiological hazardous waste facilities” in the
state, including the state’s only functioning nuclear power plant and a
French-owned facility that manufactures nuclear fuel rods. Nonetheless,
roughly 75% of the 428 claims filed since 2018 have come from the DOE’s
Hanford workers, according to the state Department of Labor and Industries.

Kathleen Kersey spent 10 years at Hanford, during both the production and
cleanup stages. Much of her work involved measuring radiation around the site
and making sure levels were safe. She says her safety training covered
radiation, but not other hazards like chemical vapors burping from the waste
tanks.

Kersey struggles to walk, has short-term memory problems and at one point lost
vision in her right eye for three months. A doctor diagnosed her with multiple
sclerosis, which is a neurological disorder, one of the categories of
illnesses the state’s presumption law recognizes as related to chemical
exposure at Hanford. In 2019 she filed a claim, which the state approved.

The DOE has appealed, arguing that something other than her time at Hanford
caused her multiple sclerosis.

Kersey is one of the 152 workers still awaiting a resolution on her workers’
compensation claim. The DOE has not paid her any back wages, she said. The DOE
declined to comment on her case.

“I feel depleted and disgusted,” Kersey said of the appeals process. “It makes
me feel like I'm worthless. I have no value.”

### “When Does This End?”

State records show that the DOE has filed more than 500 appeals since the
presumption law passed in 2018. In 20 cases, as it did with Rouse, the DOE has
appealed a single worker’s claim half a dozen times or more.

“We have seen tremendous pushback from DOE on essentially almost every single
case that's been brought,” said Washington State Attorney General Nick Brown.

Rouse’s wife, Melinda, said she knew something was wrong when he could not
remember how to cut an orange. His vision started to blur, he stumbled often,
and suddenly he felt irritable all the time. His primary care physician first
thought he might have had a brain tumor. The physician referred him to a
neurologist who noted cognitive impairment, possibly due to exposure to
multiple toxins at the Hanford Site. The neurologist then referred him to a
neuropsychologist, who diagnosed him with “toxic encephalopathy” in 2009,
saying it was “more likely than not” that chemical exposure damaged his brain,
according to court records.

Rouse at home with his wife, Melinda, and their dogs. After working at
Hanford, he developed a neurological disorder that medical experts attributed
to exposure to chemicals on the job. Lizz Giordano/Cascade PBS

The U.S. Department of Labor agreed too, approving him in 2010 for benefits
under the Energy Employees Occupational Illness Compensation Program Act,
saying it was “at least as likely as not” that Hanford contributed to his
illness. A federal medical consultant even praised the neuropsychologist who
assessed Rouse for his “unusually thorough analysis of causation.”

Rouse refiled his 2009 state workers’ compensation claim under the new law in
2018. Washington state approved it later that year.

The DOE appealed. It hired a medical toxicologist, who reviewed Rouse’s
medical records and testified that he did not have the disease he claimed, and
brought in an industrial hygienist, who downplayed the exposure risks at
Hanford. The DOE’s toxicologist testified that Rouse’s drinking was “the most
significant, what we might term, ‘toxic exposure’ that’s described in the
medical record.”

A group of three physicians and an industrial hygienist have collectively
earned over $1.7 million testifying against Hanford workers since the
presumption law’s passage, according to DOE invoices the newsrooms obtained by
a federal records request. One of the DOE’s go-to expert witness doctors
earned more than $200,000 from the DOE last year alone. He did not respond to
multiple emails seeking comment.

A single law firm, Wallace, Mann, Capener, Bishop & Debney, handles all of the
DOE’s appeals. In addition to the fees paid to expert witnesses, the
department paid the firm nearly $10 million between 2018 and 2025. The law
firm did not reply to multiple requests for comment.

In cases where the DOE has appealed the state’s approval of a claim since
2018, the agency that handles appeals has sided with workers nearly 9 times
out of 10, according to state data.

Pollet, the state representative who sponsored the 2018 presumption bill,
acknowledged that the law has fallen short of his expectation.

“This was supposed to have ended a decade ago,” he said about sick Hanford
workers still awaiting back wages and medical care. “It’s even worse than it
was 10 years ago.”

“I think their actions are not only despicable, but they are criminal,” he
said of the DOE.

The state Department of Labor and Industries said it expected “to engage
further with the DOE,” which could include putting the department on an
improvement plan and monitoring its progress.

Another option state regulators have is to revoke the DOE’s ability to accept
and pay out claims directly. According to the state Department of Labor and
Industries, the contractors that employ Hanford workers on behalf of the DOE
would then decide whether to join the state-managed fund or seek state
approval to manage claims themselves. Doing so could limit the DOE’s power to
appeal, but contractors would still have that right.

Brown, the state attorney general, said he wants to wait and see how the DOE’s
appeals of claims play out in higher courts. He hopes that once the DOE’s
losses start stacking up, it will slow the volume of its litigation.

Attorney Charlynn Hull said she thought the DOE’s approach might soften during
the Biden administration. But Hull said she observed no change in the DOE’s
behavior. Her firm, Smart Law, represents the majority of Hanford workers’
compensation claimants, including Rouse and Kersey.

One of the hardest things about the DOE’s appeals, Hull said, is the
testifying that the children and spouses of dead workers must do.

“I think that it's just, it's tormenting to them, in many ways, to relive how
awful that experience was, especially with the cancer-related death,” Hull
said. “When does this end?”

![Telephone poles and some low buildings stick up from the desert, as seen
from across the Columbia River. Mountains rise up behind the
site.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/20261013-Albaugh-
Hanford-Nuclear-Workers-
Comp-261013-0188_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=1149)A
view of the Hanford Site, which is undergoing one of the largest and most
expensive toxic waste remediation efforts in the nation's history. Margaret
Albaugh for ProPublica

### Dying While Under Appeal

For Isidoro Mata Jr., it ended with his children draining fluid from his lungs
through a tube doctors had surgically inserted into his chest.

Mata demolished buildings at Hanford for nearly 30 years. Court records show
he was diagnosed in 2015 with thyroid cancer, one of the illnesses that
Washington’s law ties to work at Hanford. Sara Chilcoat, his daughter, said he
kept working as long as he could.

State claims managers approved Mata’s claim in 2019. The DOE appealed, arguing
that “medical opinion supports denial of this claim as not related to the
distinctive conditions of employment.” The appeal did not elaborate further.
The state forced the DOE to pay his wages and the cost of his medications,
Chilcoat said. But the DOE filed a separate motion to stop his benefits while
the appeal was adjudicated.

In its motion, the DOE argued that it was likely to prevail in its appeal
because a doctor who examined Mata in 2019 believed his cancer was unrelated
to his work at Hanford, according to court records. The state found the
doctor’s examination “lacking in objective findings.”

“He was fighting for his life while they were trying to do that,” Chilcoat
said. “That makes me mad.”

Mata’s case file notes that he missed three meetings with DOE lawyers in 2020.
The state attorney general’s office sent the appeals judge a letter in July
explaining that Mata was unable to participate because of his chemotherapy
treatments. The DOE, which did not respond to questions about Mata’s case,
dropped its appeal in December.

Less than three months later, Mata died.
